To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Medicare beneficiaries with a chronic disease have a high prevalence of comorbid conditions, are at high risk for hospitalization and death, and incur a high cost for care.

the Medicare program is moving toward a chronic care program that emphasizes quality of care, that family physicians will play a key role in the success of this program, and that they will need to be active participants in its development.

the majority of older adults with chronic illnesses are satisfied with their family physician, that they perceive the family physician to be a major source of their care, that they have a strong desire to continue to be treated by their family physician as they grow older, that they have an interest in receiving care in the home, and that they are willing to pay more to receive care in the home.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: 1) the development of an integrated model of chronic care; 2) the development of a conceptual framework for understanding the organization of chronic care; and 3) the development of methods and tools to evaluate the quality of care provided to older adults with chronic disease.

the development of a new model for chronic care delivery that will be responsive to the needs of older persons with multiple chronic illnesses, and that will be financially viable for the Medicare program.
how to improve the health care system for older adults with a chronic illness, and how to improve the quality and cost-effectiveness of health care for all Americans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the US health care delivery system is in the early stages of reorganizing Medicare to provide better quality care to older adults with chronic disease, and the family physician will have a significant role in the process.
Medicare is in a state of flux, but the direction is clear.
the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act (MMA) of 2003 is a step forward, but it falls short of the mark in terms of the chronic care needs of older Americans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current health care system in the US is unsustainable and will need to be restructured.
we are at the threshold of a new era in the care of older adults with chronic illnesses, and family physicians have a critical role to play in the transformation.
the Medicare program is in transition and family medicine is in a unique position to help guide the program to its new focus on quality care for the elderly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
family physicians must be at the forefront in developing a quality care model that is person-centered, evidence-based, and focused on the trajectory of chronic illness.
the Medicare program will need to be reoriented toward chronic care.

chronic illness is a major challenge for Medicare and the US health care delivery system, and family physicians will need to play a central role in reorienting Medicare to a system that focuses on chronic illness and the quality of care.
